text: Last lesson's trade-off — row locks are cheap per-concurrency but expensive in bulk — has a limit. SQL Server handles that limit automatically, with lock escalation.

When a single statement's row or page locks on one table or index cross a threshold, roughly 5,000 locks held at once, SQL Server automatically converts all of them into a single table-level lock instead. No setting requests this. It just happens.

And here's what actually trips people up: it can happen partway through a statement. A big batch update can start out perfectly well-behaved, taking ordinary row locks that don't bother anyone, and then cross that threshold mid-execution and escalate.

The consequence is real. Sessions that were reading or writing completely unrelated rows a moment ago, and were totally fine while the update was still using row locks, suddenly start blocking once escalation kicks in — because the new table lock covers every row, not just the ones the update actually cares about. This is one of the most common real causes of a whole application appearing to freeze for thirty seconds.

There's no flag to disable escalation. The practical fix is to break a large batch operation into smaller batches, each comfortably under the lock-count threshold, so no single statement ever accumulates enough locks to trigger it.
Next up: a lesson you'll come back to constantly on the job — sys.dm_tran_locks, the real dynamic management view for seeing exactly which locks are held, by whom, right now.
